paras: The lynching of Henry Foster was the hanging of a Black hired man by members of a citizen pursuing party near Lansing Switch, six miles east of Longview, Texas, on the night of June 7, 1888. Foster had been accused of attempting to assault an elderly white woman near Friendship three days earlier, and the white Texas press reported his death as deserved punishment.

According to a Longview dispatch dated June 4, a Black stranger who had worked only a few days for Colonel A. M. McMellan, six miles north of Longview near Friendship, was accused of entering the room of Mrs. E. A. McMellan at 1 a.m. and attempting to "outrage" her. The report said he had first hidden the colonel's double-barrel shotgun, fled when the older man intervened, and took the gun and ammunition with him. He had given his name as Henry Foster but told others it was Tol Dager and that he came from Louisiana; the dispatch described him as very black, about 178 pounds, and blind in the right eye.

The colonel raised his neighbors, who joined the search. The same dispatch warned that the fugitive "must know that capture means death," since "no jail or court-house" would shelter him if the citizens caught him.

A second Longview dispatch, dated June 8, said the pursuing party came upon Foster late the previous evening at Lansing Switch on the Texas and Pacific railroad, near the line between Harrison and Gregg counties. He was sitting on the tracks with the colonel's gun across his lap when four men came up silently behind him and disarmed him. Black residents nearby saw him led into a skirt of woods but were afraid to follow, and when they went there at 8 o'clock the next morning they found him hanging from a tree.

By noon the body was still hanging, and the correspondent wrote that no officers had been notified and that no one seemed willing to touch it. No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage, and the men who hanged Foster were not named.

The episode was covered only in white Texas papers, chiefly through specials from a Longview correspondent. Even before the capture, the Fort Worth Daily Gazette headlined the first report "A Negro Attacks a White Woman Near Longview—Judge Lynch after Him," and the Austin Weekly Statesman ran the same text two days later as "A Negro Fiend." The Gazette's report of the killing, "A Ghastly Spectacle," dwelt on the bloated body "covered with green flies" and concluded that "the ravisher has met his just dues at last."

The San Antonio Daily Light reduced the story to one line among its state news: "The rape fiend Foster is caught and lynched at Longview." The Austin Weekly Statesman printed the June 8 dispatch a week later under "Ravisher Captured and Lynched," in a version that called Foster the "ravisher of three white women," a charge absent from the Gazette's text and unexplained in either paper.
The family's name appears as McMellan, McMillan and McWilliams, and Foster's alias as Tol Dager, Tol Tager and Tal Degar, variations that likely reflect telegraph or typesetting errors.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Foster
bases: A Black man accused of attempting to assault a white woman was seized by four men of a pursuing party and found hanged the next morning, with no officers involved [A3, A5].

Foster was taken by four men of a citizen pursuing party and found hanged, with no officers notified, in punishment for an alleged attempted assault on a white woman [A3, A5]; the San Antonio Light called it a lynching [A4].

The capture and hanging rest on one Longview dispatch of June 8 printed in two papers [A3, A5], and the one-line San Antonio brief adds no independent detail [A4]; the earlier accusation likewise comes from one Longview text printed twice [A1, A2].

accounts.label: Longview correspondent, June 4
accounts.gist: A Black hired man hid the colonel's shotgun, entered Mrs. McMellan's room at night and tried to assault her, fled when the colonel intervened, and was being hunted by neighbors who would not let a jail shelter him.

accounts.label: Longview correspondent, June 8 (from Black witnesses)
accounts.gist: Four men of the pursuing party surprised Foster resting on the railroad at Lansing Switch, disarmed him and took him into the woods, where Black residents found him hanged the next morning.

The Statesman ran the same text under 'A NEGRO FIEND Attempts to Outrage an Old Lady in East Texas'.
'A Ghastly Spectacle. The Rape Fiend, Foster, is Lynched Near Longview' described the bloated body and said 'the ravisher has met his just dues at last'.
